source_refs.note: Topic 18.9.1 with the Interesting Information box (PDF 31-32); Figures 18.11 and 18.12 are replaced by original diagrams (the book's Figure 18.12 shows two drawings of each isomer). The book's octahedral example [Co(NH3)4Cl2] is given with its charge, +.

blocks.text: In cis-trans isomers identical ligands are either next to each other (at 90 degrees, cis) or opposite each other (at 180 degrees, trans). This is common in square planar complexes, e.g. [Pt(NH3)2Cl2], and in octahedral complexes, e.g. [Co(NH3)4Cl2]+.

In cis-[Pt(NH3)2Cl2] (cisplatin) the chlorine atoms are adjacent, at 90 degrees; in trans-[Pt(NH3)2Cl2] (transplatin) they are opposite, at 180 degrees. The two isomers have different properties: cisplatin is an anticancer drug, while transplatin is not. In transplatin the bond dipoles of the identical ligands point in opposite directions and cancel, so the molecule is non-polar; in cisplatin they do not cancel, giving a dipole moment, so it is polar.

blocks.alt: Two square planar sketches of [Pt(NH3)2Cl2]. Left, cis-platin: the two Cl at neighbouring corners, 90 degrees apart, labelled polar. Right, trans-platin: the two Cl at opposite corners, 180 degrees apart, labelled non-polar.
blocks.caption: The geometrical isomers cisplatin and transplatin (original diagram after Figure 18.11).
blocks.long_description: Both isomers have the same formula and the same bonds. In cis-platin the two chlorine atoms are next to each other (90 degrees), so the bond dipoles do not cancel and the molecule is polar. In trans-platin they are opposite (180 degrees), the dipoles cancel and the molecule is non-polar. Only cis-platin is an anticancer drug.

blocks.title: Interesting information: cisplatin
blocks.text: Cisplatin, cis-diamminedichloroplatinum(II), is a landmark anticancer drug. It was discovered by accident, when platinum electrodes were found to stop bacterial cells from dividing. Inside a rapidly dividing cancer cell water replaces its chloride ligands; the activated drug then binds to guanine bases in DNA and cross-links the strands, which blocks DNA replication and triggers programmed cell death (apoptosis).
[Co(NH3)4(H2O)2]3+ is an [MA4B2] octahedral complex. In its cis isomer the two H2O ligands are adjacent, at 90 degrees; in the trans isomer they are opposite, at 180 degrees.

blocks.alt: Two octahedral sketches of [Co(NH3)4(H2O)2]3+, an [MA4B2] complex. Left (cis): the two H2O ligands, in red, are on neighbouring positions at 90 degrees. Right (trans): they are on opposite positions, above and below the Co, at 180 degrees. The four NH3 ligands are blue.
blocks.caption: Cis and trans isomers of [Co(NH3)4(H2O)2]3+ (original diagram after Figure 18.12).
blocks.long_description: An octahedral complex of the type [MA4B2] can exist as cis and trans isomers. In cis-[Co(NH3)4(H2O)2]3+ the two water ligands occupy adjacent positions at 90 degrees; in the trans isomer they occupy opposite positions at 180 degrees.

blocks.prompt: Which isomer of [Pt(NH3)2Cl2] is polar, and why?
blocks.explanation: The cis isomer: its two Pt-Cl bond dipoles are at 90 degrees and do not cancel, so the molecule has a dipole moment.

items: cis: identical ligands at 90 degrees; trans: at 180 degrees.
Cisplatin is polar and an anticancer drug; transplatin is non-polar.
Octahedral [MA4B2] complexes such as [Co(NH3)4(H2O)2]3+ also show cis-trans isomerism.
